deep.reconstruction:
The page has two 7-place tables, each argued at 0°, 6°, ..., 90°, with full difference schemes.

TABLE 1, with column 1 = f(θ).
- Values: f(0) = 0.3826834 = sin(π/8) and f(90°) = 1/2.
- Identification (mine, verified at every row): f(θ)·cos θ = sin(22.5°·(1 − (θ/90°)^2)).
  - Spot checks: θ=30° gives sin 20°; θ=60° gives sin 12.5°; θ=6° gives sin 22.4°.
  - In radians: f(θ) = sin(π/8 − θ^2/(2π)) / cos θ.
  - At θ = π/2 the quotient is 0/0, and the limit is 1/2, which is the tabulated value.
- Link to the Riemann–Siegel formula. Put θ = 2π(p − 1/2), i.e. p = 1/2 + θ/360°. Then
  f = cos(2π(p^2 − p − 1/16)) / cos(2πp) = Ψ(p).
  This is the leading coefficient C0(p) of the Riemann–Siegel remainder, in the form Siegel (1932) extracted from Riemann's Nachlass.
  - Ψ is even about p = 1/2.
  - The table covers p ∈ [1/2, 3/4], hence by symmetry [1/4, 3/4], in steps of 1/60.
- The remaining columns are the difference table: Δ1, Δ2, then Δ3 and Δ4 in units of 1e-7.
  - The 0° row uses evenness, f(−6°) = f(6°). That is why the 6° row shows Δ2 = 2·0.0004860 = 0.0009720.
  - It is also why the 12° row shows Δ3 = 19 and Δ4 = 38 = 2·19.
  - Fourth differences run steadily at about 32–41 and then fall to about 18–26 near 90°. This is a smoothness/accuracy check of the computation.

TABLE 2, with column 1 = g(θ).
- Values: g(0) = 0 and g(90°) = 1/2.
- Identification (mine, verified at every row): g(θ) = f(θ)·sin θ = tan θ · sin(π/8 − θ^2/(2π)).
  - For example g(30°) = f(30°)/2 and g(6°)/f(6°) = sin 6°.
  - Thus (f cos θ, f sin θ) are the Cartesian components of the point with polar coordinates (Ψ, θ).
  - Equivalently, g = −Ψ(p)·sin 2πp.
- The purpose of g is not stated (perhaps auxiliary for interpolation or a curve plot; my conjecture).
- Its difference table is also complete.
  - The second differences are entered as positive numbers although they are negative (the function is concave).
  - The 6° row has Δ2 = 0 and the 12° row has Δ4 = 0, by oddness, g(−θ) = −g(θ).

All differences in both tables check exactly, except one slip in the 84° line of Table 1 (see errors).
errors: Table 1, 84° row: the value reads 0.4840117, but the true value is 0.4840112. The differences actually used (Δ1 = 0.0146633, then 0.0159889 at 90°, Δ2 = 0.0012814, 0.0013256) correspond to 0.4840111, which sums to 0.5000000 at 90°. So either the 84° entry is a copying slip (7 for 1), or the image shows an ambiguous digit. With 0.4840117, the true first differences would have been 0.0146639 and 0.0159883.

No other arithmetic errors: all first through fourth differences in both tables check to the last unit, and the tabulated values agree with sin(π/8−θ^2/(2π))/cos θ and its product with sin θ to about ±1e-7.
Minor notational point: in Table 2 the second differences (negative) are recorded without sign, so the Δ3 and Δ4 columns are of the absolute values.

results.what: 7-place table with full difference scheme of Ψ(p)=cos(2π(p²−p−1/16))/cos(2πp), written as sin(π/8−θ²/2π)/cos θ with θ=2π(p−1/2), for p from 1/2 to 3/4 in steps of 1/60
results.modern_name: Riemann–Siegel coefficient C0(p) (Ψ(p)) of the Riemann–Siegel formula
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Nachlass), published and analysed by C. L. Siegel 1932; Ψ tables later by Titchmarsh/Comrie, Haselgrove, and others

results.what: Companion table g = Ψ·sin θ = −Ψ(p) sin 2πp with difference scheme, exploiting oddness at θ=0
results.modern_name: auxiliary (polar component) table of the Riemann–Siegel coefficient

results.what: Use of parity (even and odd extension) to start difference tables at the origin, and fourth differences as an accuracy check

deep.surprise_reason: The function Ψ(p) is already known, through Siegel 1932, to come from Riemann's Nachlass, and Riemann is known to have done numerical zeta computations. A carefully differenced 7-place numerical table of Ψ in his hand is a notable unpublished computational detail that confirms he worked it out numerically. It is not a new theoretical result.

checkable.asserts: the tabulated f equals the Riemann–Siegel Ψ(p) with θ = 2π(p−1/2) (should simplify to 0)
